threads.title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading

reactions.author: yurimo
reactions.text:
Respectfully to the authors and to everyone here, I ask you to actually read the paper before losing your mind, or at the very least plug it into Claude. It is a cool project but not as nearly as insane as people say. I think the blog writing and subsequent posting overstate the results.

Part of my research is in weight space learning. For starters, we have had the ability to edit weights, to generate new weights, to identify weights for a while. Here is an example for larger models as early as 2023:
https://rome.baulab.info/

Weight space interpretability and learning is an active research community, has been for the past 3 years with many great papers. I suspect it is hitting non-interp folks harder because the authors hyped up their work, and people who are not in the field did not bother to read it before typing up X posts.

Some experiments here are done on very small models (20K params). We already know that small models are more interpretable. In fact, much of editing here you can do by hand. For Qwen, the model fixed a looping bug that may have been known apriori, and it is basically a steering vector, a very established technique. This is clear when they then attempt to "improve" math capability, and it doesn't work. For me, this paper rather shows that OpenAI has done training on mechinterp  environment, in fact, maybe even on weight space learning datasets, which are open. But it does not show some insane "well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional alg…

reactions.author: vessenes
reactions.text:
This is insane.

Astra can, without tooling, determine what games small networks are trained on, can edit the weights of networks directly to improve outcomes, and can hand edit a small qwen model to improve its math skills by like 5x.

I'm shook. If you'd asked me this morning whether LLMs have native understanding of their weights that is less than human <-> neuron understanding, the same as human or more than human, I would have said "same to less" depending on definitions.

No human can go edit a brain to become better at math. This is just very, very surprising to me and extremely interesting. I would guess this upsets quite a number of interp theories and philosophical takes on what's going on with these networks.

reactions.author: xg15
reactions.text:
And here we go...

As others have said, while still absolutely insane, I don't find it completely out-of-the-blue surprising. One of the recurring abilities of (current-generation) LLMs seem to be to rapidly grasp very complex systems, where humans would need months or years to reach the same level of expertise.

You can see this in the way a coding agent can "understand" and explain sprawling legacy codebases in seconds.

You can also see it in the projects that are using them to reverse-engineer proprietary IoT protocols or computer games.

But those were all systems where we had detailed knowledge about what structures are there to be reverse-enginered.

If the models can transfer this ability to some other systems where we don't know the underlying structure then I think we will be in for a lot more craziness in the future. (Protein interaction networks? DNA sequences? Ecosystem interactions? Animal languages?)

As for weights, if the models really can analyze the semantics behind specific weights or directions, I have my hopes that they could also give a textual explanation or help designing tools to make "handcrafting" weights more practical in general.

reactions.author: jsenn
reactions.text:
I feel like this is conflating 2 separate results in a slightly misleading way.

> We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights

This claim is backed up by the ability of Astra, given a text representation of the weights of tiny (20k) special-purpose models, to figure out what those models do and in some cases improve them beyond what RL could do just by reading the weights with no tool calls. They call this "weight-space programming".

> Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights

Here it did use tool calls, and seemingly used standard steering vector techniques to identify and fix reasoning loops in this small Qwen model. This doesn't seem that related to the previous results.

Showerthoughts:

1. If you know ANN or, say, perceptron, you know you can eyeball models too. You can even have certain strategies in composing your own network. This weight-space programming thing is nothing new in that sense, and the article doesn’t really provide much beyond “LLM can do it”. That’s not even science…

2. I’m pretty sure this is Transformers thing, not even LLM. Transformer is, by itself, good at finding patterns in relatively-larger data. So this is unlikely limited to Astra.

3. This approach quickly becomes impractical as the scale goes up. Sure, you can also have multiple models chained with fewer connections, but, now that’s what we’ve been doing for years.

All in all, yeah, an interesting find, but too far from changing the game. Over-exaggerated every way. Perhaps one should start from formulating what weight-space programming is, what methodologies, practicality, etc. LLM bench is one of the last things you need.

reactions.author: Aurornis
reactions.text:
LLMs have been used to investigate and improve LLMs for a long time. Drawing parallels to human brains and neurons isn't all that interesting other than as a philosophical abstraction.

The work done in this experiment could have also been done by a sufficiently motivated human with enough time to explore, though obviously we would need more tools to visualize and track things. There have been a lot of interesting LLM introspection tools that allow you to peek into the model and see what's being activated and run experiments to trigger it.

Are you familiar with abliterated or "uncensored" models where weights have been modified to avoid triggering refusal patterns? You take an LLM, create test cases that trigger the refusal pattern, observe weights involved in that response, then tweak those weights until the response is reduced. This is the same type of work, applied to a specific type of error that was impeding math within Qwen. That work can also be done with an LLM in a harness running the experiments. The amazing part here is that Astra was large enough to walk through the problem without other tooling doing it experimentally.

So I don't think your analogy of a human modifying a neuron is quite applicable. LLM weights are not neurons and they've been inspectable, by humans or LLMs in a harness, for a long time.

reactions.author: honnibal.dev
reactions.text:
Stage magicians often do the same trick multiple ways. One iteration uses a gimmick prop, the next one shows you the prop isn’t gimmick but that one palms the object, the third time was a forced choice etc. When you watch the performance you assume there’s only one technique, so each time they do it they seem to debunk your hypothesis about how it must be working.

This is pretty much how the experiments in the ‘Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen’ post work. The post’s abstract says:

> Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

> Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

If you read that, would you assume that the Qwen experiment worked ‘just by looking at the raw weights’? Well it doesn’t. There’s experiments that look at raw weights, and experiments that improve a game-playing network, and an experiment that improves Qwen at maths. But those latter two aren’t just working with raw weights, they write Python programs.

Here’s a summary of what the post actually does and how the techniques work.

¹ Given one recorded episode of the failure. ² In one try, changing 3.5% of the weights. ³ Weights start at zero, so there’s nothing to read. ⁴ Beats PPO-500M only on Breakout (517 vs. 25); loses to it on Seaquest (53 vs. 89) and Asterix (53 vs. 55). ⁵ Runs up to 16 texts and sees only the attention patterns, not the outputs.

The “just by looking at the raw weights” setting (raw floats in context, no tools, no running the network) only appears in experiments 1, 2 and 4, on networks of 17K–172K weights. Every experiment involving a real language model uses Python, and the Qwen result, which is the headline one, also gets to run the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems.

What the Qwen result actually shows is that Astra can be prompted to devise and perform tasks that a human ML engineer could do. Human ML engineers write snippets of code that analyse or even modify network weights “directly” all the time. Figuring out how to do this productively is not nothing, and AI models of a year or two ago would have failed at all these tasks.

But to me the Qwen result and the other experiments that use Python don’t belong in the same post or paper as the experiments that read the weights directly. A single technique that could achieve both, “Author weights for a small game from scratch” and “Improve the performance of a large model on a sample task” would imply a deep capability. If you test a single technique that way you’ve demonstrated a sort of ‘gestalt’ of the weights (it can write them out from scratch) and also that it understands a large existing network. But that’s not at all true here, because it’s not a single technique.

reactions.author: x313
reactions.text:
I work in this field (mech interp research) and I agree, the original post is definitely misleading. Some overselling in research is normal but it's a bit much.

First, the key result has nothing to do with making Qwen better at math, it just reduces reasoning loops.

Reasoning loops are a simple problem: the model generates the </think> token (which closes reasoning) with too low probability. You can fix this with simple steering approaches where you add a vector to different components of the LLM (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22048, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18167, etc). The method Astra used for identifying the vector is the standard procedure humans use (contrastive analysis). Such steering vector creation is basically the standard "intro-level interp project" for human researchers.

If you can code and understand LLM internals, you can do this yourself in 4-8 hours. The SWE equivalent would be doing binary patching with a debugger. Cool that frontier models can do this, but not unexpected since humans can do it without issue.

Speaking for myself. I’ve been aware of a lot of concepts around training, but stayed away from it until very recently.

A few weeks ago, I formed a hypothesis that I could get a smaller model good at the specific standards I have for my git commit messages, which are hard to get out of most LLMs today.

I spent the last four to five weeks on traditional training. It improved in a lot of areas, but not enough to be usable for me.

Yesterday, the article the author of this post is critical of gave me enough of an aha that maybe the problems I was seeing could be solved by having a larger LLM change the weights directly, without going through training.

In the last twelve-ish hours I’ve made more headway than I have in 2+ weeks. I’m using one of my last well performing checkpoints (full fine-tune + changes to the decision head/LoRA, etc.) and gave the model free rein to change any of the layers.

Its last two actions: (a) removed 16 participant-order directions from a head matrix, which improved one type of reasoning and degraded another, and (b) restored one of the 16, which reversed the degradation while keeping the core improvement.

All that to say, this might be known to people who’ve been around training for years, even decades, but it’s new to a lot of us. And we’re excited about it.
